A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same REFORM study. Their main text, appendices, equations, figures, tables, and algorithm descriptions are readable and support reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original retrieval, long-context benchmark, multimodal, ablation, embedding-head, and computational-efficiency experiments.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical results and adds broader benchmark evaluation, code completion, pooling ablations, latency breakdowns, and larger-model experiments.

M1.justification: The compression, early exit, normalized head-embedding combination, similarity search, pooling, gathering, and KV recomputation procedure remains unchanged. The expanded head-selection explanation documents the existing procedure, and the code-model experiments apply it without introducing a new component.

E1.justification: V2 expands ∞-Bench from four English text tasks to ten, adding passkey, number and key-value retrieval, Chinese QA, code debugging, and mathematical finding. RepoEval adds repository-level API and line completion. These substantially broaden language, domain, and task coverage beyond the retained benchmarks.

E2.justification: V1 Figure 3 compares REFORM with H2O, InfiniPot, and InfLLM on NIAH; v2 retains only REFORM's heatmap and removes those comparisons. The principal benchmark and RAG comparator sets otherwise remain unchanged, and the added experiments use existing comparator methods.

E3.justification: New protocols include RepoEval with Qwen2.5-Coder 1.5B/7B, repository context excluding the target file, and edit-similarity scoring; Qwen2.5-32B evaluation; and separate prefill/decoding measurements on H200 with 200 generated tokens at 256k, 512k, and 1M contexts. The original H100, 10-token efficiency experiment remains, so these are additional settings rather than replacements.

E4.justification: V2 Table 6a adds sensitivity tests reducing the default 129-token pooling window to 5 and 17 tokens, testing the importance of preserving neighboring context. Appendix D.2 adds prefill/decoding and compress-plus-gather/recomputation latency breakdowns across context lengths. These materially extend the existing component and efficiency analyses; the original compression and head-selection ablations are retained.

E5.justification: V2 Table 8 specifies averaging over 20 runs for the new H200 latency measurements. The retained H100 experiment still reports averaging over 10 samples; this does not establish an increase in runs for that experiment. Neither version supplies confidence intervals, dispersion estimates, or significance tests.

E6.justification: V2 adds substantial benchmark, pooling, latency, and 32B-model results. For example, RepoEval 1.5B API completion scores 65.3 for REFORM versus 61.8 for InfLLM. The Mistral ∞-Bench average changes from 31.2 to 50.2 because coverage expands from four to ten tasks; all four shared task columns are unchanged. Matched RULER, BABILong, MM-NIAH, RAG, and H100 efficiency scores remain unchanged. NIAH baseline heatmaps and BABILong across-length averages are removed.

T1.justification: Appendix E.1 adds asymptotic reasoning under bounded chunk/query assumptions, assigning REFORM linear time and memory and contrasting recurrent and random-access baselines. The existing MNR definition and embedding-concatenation equation remain unchanged. Appendix E.2 supplies conceptual motivation for head selection, without a new theorem or proof.

C1.justification: The main framework, efficiency, and modality-generality claims remain. V2 adds an explicit superiority claim for repository-level code completion and revises the headline RULER/BABILong gains from over 50%/27% to over 52%/34%. The underlying RULER/BABILong tables are unchanged, so these numerical revisions do not demonstrate improved method performance.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive explanations linking pooling to contextual preservation, faster decoding to the smaller recomputed cache, and complementary heads to structural versus semantic retrieval. Section 5 newly discusses gathering reliability and redundant attention-score computation with Flash Attention. Appendices D.2 and E expand the interpretation of efficiency and head specialization beyond v1's narrower discussion.

D1.justification: V2 lists exact head/layer choices for both Qwen2.5-Coder models, discloses redundant attention-score matrix multiplication, estimates offline head-selection cost, and adds dataset/model license information. The previously specified Mistral, Qwen-7B, and Pixtral head choices and cache budgets remain unchanged.

R1.justification: V2 adds RepoCoder and literature connecting head selection to mechanistic interpretability, intermediate representations, and hybrid retrieval. The earlier text-embedding and Landmark Attention references disappear with edited passages. These extend the supporting rationale while retaining the central positioning against recurrent compression and random-access methods.

P1.justification: V2 substantially reorganizes the narrative: Algorithm 1 moves to Appendix A, appendix ablations move into Section 4.5, and realistic-text, code, and multimodal evaluations are consolidated in Section 4.3. Introduction and method explanations are revised, and the supplementary material gains separate discussion, impacts, and licensing sections.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two-column to single-column presentation. RULER and BABILong tables are merged, RepoEval is combined with MM-NIAH, and ablation/efficiency tables become paired panels. Figure 3 shrinks from four comparator heatmaps to one, while new latency and larger-model tables extend the appendix displays.

improvement.justification: The broader realistic-task and larger-model evaluations substantially strengthen v1's evidence for general applicability. Pooling sensitivity and stage-specific latency measurements address previously untested aspects of gathering and computational cost, while new limitations and implementation disclosures improve transparency. These gains outweigh the loss of the NIAH baseline panels. The improvement rests on stronger validation and explanation, not the higher ∞-Bench average produced by changing task coverage.
